title: Regulatory, Quality and Compliance
answer: Regulators on both sides of the Atlantic now set out how AI should be used in medicine development. The FDA asks sponsors to show a model is credible for its specific context of use, the EMA has a reflection paper covering the whole medicine lifecycle, Europe has drafted the first GMP annex written for AI, and the EU AI Act adds its own duties for high risk systems.

sections.body: Treat every AI model that touches a regulated decision as something to qualify: define the question it answers, the context it is used in, how much the decision depends on it, and the evidence that it performs. The same discipline satisfies the FDA framework, the EMA reflection paper and the draft Annex 22.
sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences team

siblings.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

explainer:
Regulation decides how far AI can be trusted in a life sciences company. A drug or device maker is responsible for every piece of evidence it submits and every decision it makes about quality and safety, and that responsibility does not move to a software vendor when an AI system is involved.

Regulators approach AI through context of use. The question is never simply whether a model is accurate, but what decision it supports, how much that decision depends on it, and what would happen if it were wrong. A model that drafts an internal summary needs little formal evidence. A model that selects trial patients, measures an outcome or decides whether a batch is released needs a documented case that it works for exactly that purpose, tested on independent data and controlled when it changes.

Three bodies of rules now apply together. In the United States the FDA has proposed a risk based credibility framework for AI in drug and biologic submissions, and has long standing rules for electronic records and computerised systems. In Europe the EMA has a reflection paper covering the whole lifecycle, the GMP rules are gaining an annex written specifically for AI, and the EU AI Act adds horizontal duties, starting with AI literacy for staff. The FDA and EMA have also agreed shared principles, which makes a single global approach realistic.

The practical result is that validation, documentation and change control, familiar disciplines in this industry, are now the core of AI governance.
key_points: Context of use and model risk decide how much evidence an AI model needs.
The FDA credibility framework, EMA reflection paper and draft GMP Annex 22 apply alongside existing Part 11 and Annex 11 rules.
The EU AI Act adds AI literacy and, for medical devices, high risk duties.
The FDA and EMA share ten good AI practice principles.
The sponsor stays accountable for every AI assisted record and submission.
